title: U.S. teens remain optimistic about solving national problems while civic and economic knowledge and opportunities to practice participation lag
source_unit: U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation, 2026 Civic and Economic Literacy Survey, conducted with RXN
geography: United States; 1,000 registered adult voters and 1,000 teens ages 13–17

observations.period: 2026 survey; U.S. teens and registered adult voters

denominator.unit: 1,000 registered adult voters and 1,000 teens ages 13–17

issues_can_be_fixed_teens.unit: percent of teens saying issues they believe deserve national attention can eventually be fixed

issues_can_be_fixed_adults.unit: percent of adults saying issues they believe deserve national attention can eventually be fixed

see_political_division_teens.unit: percent of teens saying America is politically divided

see_political_division_adults.unit: percent of adults saying America is politically divided

observations.method: National Civic and Economic Literacy Survey conducted in partnership with RXN; the public article reports separate teen and adult samples and selected civic-attitude comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The public article does not provide full questionnaire wording, sampling details or subgroup margins; optimism is an attitude measure and does not establish actual problem-solving capacity, participation or future behavior.
observations.subgroup: U.S. teens ages 13–17 and registered adult voters.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher teen optimism alongside awareness of division may signal constructive agency, but it may also reflect distance from adult institutional responsibility or limited experience with policy constraints.

observations.period: 2026 survey; civic values versus perceived civic performance

denominator.unit: 1,000 registered adult voters and 1,000 teens ages 13–17

listening_important_adults.unit: percent of adults saying listening to people with different viewpoints is important

listening_important_teens.unit: percent of teens saying listening to people with different viewpoints is important

listening_works_well_both.unit: percent of both adults and teens saying the country is doing well at listening across viewpoints

small_business_favorable.value: 91% of adults and 90% of teens view small businesses favorably

observations.method: Survey questions on civic values, perceived institutional performance and views of local business, reported as adult-versus-teen comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: Importance and perceived performance are not behavioral measures; favorable views of small business do not show that local firms create civic trust or that respondents support specific firms or policies.
observations.subgroup: U.S. teens ages 13–17 and registered adult voters.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap between valuing listening and seeing it practiced points toward an opportunity for repeated settings to practice disagreement, but the survey does not test which settings work.

denominator.unit: 1,000 registered adult voters and 1,000 teens ages 13–17

civic_knowledge_pass_adults.unit: percent of adults answering at least six of ten civic questions correctly

civic_knowledge_pass_teens.unit: percent of teens answering at least six of ten civic questions correctly

economic_literacy_pass_adults.unit: percent of adults answering at least five of eight economic questions correctly

economic_literacy_pass_teens.unit: percent of teens answering at least five of eight economic questions correctly

high_literacy.value: Only about one in ten adults and teens demonstrated the strongest levels of economic literacy measured

observations.method: Civic and economic knowledge questions in the 2026 survey; pass thresholds are reported by the Chamber Foundation article.
observations.uncertainty: The public article does not show the full test items, scoring model or psychometric validation; passing a short knowledge test is not equivalent to informed political judgment or economic security.
observations.subgroup: U.S. teens ages 13–17 and registered adult voters.
observations.counterinterpretation: The knowledge gap may be partly addressable through education, but information alone may not overcome time, access, institutional distrust, language, economic pressure or lack of meaningful participation routes.

observations.period: 2026 survey; civic engagement as practice and institutional pathway

denominator.unit: 1,000 registered adult voters and 1,000 teens ages 13–17

government_and_local_business_importance.unit: percent of teens saying understanding government, supporting local businesses and listening to different viewpoints are important to national success

formal_practice_gap.value: The article identifies a gap between civic interest and actual opportunities to practice listening, tradeoff assessment, disagreement and problem-solving

workplace_bridge.value: The Foundation frames employers and workplaces as settings where civic understanding, collaboration and constructive disagreement can be practiced

observations.method: Survey interpretation and program framing in a Chamber Foundation publication; the pathway from civic education or workplace practice to later participation is proposed, not evaluated.
observations.uncertainty: The article is produced by an organization that promotes employer and civic-learning programs; it does not provide a randomized intervention, longitudinal follow-up or independent test of program effects.
observations.subgroup: Young people, adults, schools, employers, local businesses, communities and civic institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Workplaces and businesses can create low-friction civic practice, but they may also shape civic participation around employer priorities or substitute private programs for public education infrastructure.

related_sources.claim: Companion publication connecting the 2026 Chamber Foundation survey with College Board findings on youth civic interest, formal political engagement and practice gaps.
Prior-year survey context on confidence-versus-knowledge gaps and the Chamber Foundation's civic-learning framing.

boundary: This record captures a U.S. civic-capacity transition: teens and adults recognize division and value civic skills, but knowledge, perceived performance and opportunities to practice participation do not keep pace with stated importance. It is a Chamber Foundation/RXN survey and program-framing publication, not an independent probability-sample estimate, causal civic-education evaluation, longitudinal participation study or proof that employer and business programs produce democratic outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official U.S. Chamber Foundation publication and companion civic-engagement page were reviewed for sample composition, teen-adult optimism comparisons, civic values, perceived listening performance, civic and economic knowledge, local-business sentiment, formal-engagement gaps and program boundaries; the retrieved HTML publication was hashed.
